title: Rules of inference and equivalences
note: Some argument forms are valid in every instance. Modus ponens and modus tollens work from a conditional, hypothetical syllogism chains conditionals, and disjunctive syllogism eliminates an option. A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, not its converse. De Morgan's laws: ¬(P ∧ Q) equals ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and ¬(P ∨ Q) equals ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

read.title: Patterns you can trust
text: Some argument patterns are valid no matter what you plug into them. The two most famous work from a conditional, 'If P then Q'. Modus ponens affirms the antecedent: P is true, so Q is. Modus tollens denies the consequent: Q is false, so P is false too. If the alarm sounds whenever there is smoke, and the alarm is silent, there is no smoke (assuming the alarm works as the premise says).
Hypothetical syllogism links conditionals into a chain: if P then Q, and if Q then R, so if P then R. Disjunctive syllogism rules out an option: P or Q, not P, so Q.

Equivalences let you rewrite a sentence without changing its meaning. A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, 'If not Q, then not P'. It is not equivalent to its converse, 'If Q, then P', or its inverse, 'If not P, then not Q'; confusing them produces the fallacies in the next unit.

De Morgan's laws tell you how negation passes through 'and' and 'or'. Saying a person is not both rich and famous means the person is either not rich or not famous. Wanting neither tea nor coffee means wanting no tea and no coffee. Negation flips 'and' to 'or' and 'or' to 'and'.
